before.stem: ww Transection of the anterolateral tract of the spinal cord results in which of the following clinical features:
options: Cerebellar incoordination (Vv) Loss of pain and temperature sensation 1%
Loss of vibration and fine-touch sensation
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: Transection of the anterolateral tract results in contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensations, starting one segment below the lesion. . v Spinal Cord Tracts ANATOMY / CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM

after.stem: Transection of the anterolateral tract of the spinal cord results in which of the following clinical features:
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensation
Loss of vibration and fine-touch sensation
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: The anterolateral/spinothalamic system carries pain and temperature; interruption produces a contralateral deficit beginning below the lesion.

before.stem: ww A 65 year old lady presents to ED complaining of sudden onset visual loss. On examination you demonstrate visual loss on the right side of the vertical midline with macular sparing in both eyes. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely occluded:
before.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. A lesion to this area will result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. . Vv Arterial Supply of Brain

after.stem: A 65 year old lady presents to ED complaining of sudden onset visual loss. On examination you demonstrate visual loss on the right side of the vertical midline with macular sparing in both eyes. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely occluded:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex; infarction can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
after.learningNote: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex; infarction can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
after.highYieldNote: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex; infarction can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

memoryAid.coreFact: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex; infarction can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

evidence.externalFinding: The posterior-circulation reference supports PCA supply to the occipital visual cortex.

before.stem: ww A 65 year old lady , with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, presents to ED with a 1 hour history of sudden onset of weakness and numbness solely in her left leg and foot. She is placed on the stroke pathway. Which of the following blood vessels has most likely been occluded:
options: Anterior cerebral artery (x) Posterior cerebral artery 4%
before.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cerebral hemisphere including the paracentral lobule which is formed from portions of the frontal and parietal lobes, and responsible for the motor and sensory function of the lower limb. v

after.stem: A 65 year old lady, with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, presents to ED with a 1 hour history of sudden onset of weakness and numbness solely in her left leg and foot. She is placed on the stroke pathway. Which of the following blood vessels has most likely been occluded:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the paracentral lobule for contralateral lower-limb motor and sensory function.
after.learningNote: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the paracentral lobule for contralateral lower-limb motor and sensory function.
after.highYieldNote: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the paracentral lobule for contralateral lower-limb motor and sensory function.

memoryAid.coreFact: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the paracentral lobule for contralateral lower-limb motor and sensory function.

warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: The triceps tendon reflex tap predominantly tests spinal cord segment C7. Vv Myotomes and Reflexes ANATOMY / CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM / LOWER LIMB / INNERVATION OF LOWER LIMB /

before.stem: ww The primary visual cortex is located in which of the following regions: (/) Occipital lobe 89% (x) Parietal lobe 2%

before.explanation: The primary visual cortex is located within the occipital lobe and together with the visual association cortex is responsible for vision. ‘ . Vv Occipital Lobe ANATOMY / CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM

before.stem: w What type of visual field defect are you likely to see in a lesion of the visual cortex:
options: Monocular blindness (Vv) Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing 41%
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: A lesion of the visual cortex will result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. . Vv Visual Pathway ANATOMY / CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM / CRANIAL NERVE LESIONS

options: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

before.stem: Ww A patient complains of diplopia on reading or walking downstairs, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected: & Trochlear nerve 70%
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve 2%
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: Trochlear nerve palsy causes weakness of downward gaze. The patient complains of difficulty reading or walking downstairs and of vertical diplopia. The eye is extorted and may be elevated and the patient may head tilt to the opposite side of the palsy to compensate. Vv

after.stem: A patient complains of diplopia on reading or walking downstairs, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected:

after.explanation: Trochlear nerve palsy weakens the superior oblique, causing impaired downward gaze and vertical diplopia, often noticed when reading or walking downstairs.

before.stem: A 64 year old lady complains of a sore right eye. On examination, you note a normal corneal blink reflex on her left side but no consensual blink reflex on her right side. A lesion in which of the following structures is most likely to cause this clinical picture:
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: The corneal blink reflex is an involuntary blinking of the eyelids, mediated by the orbicularis oculi muscle, and elicited by stimulation of the cornea. The afferent pathway is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and the efferent pathway is the facial nerve. Loss of the consensual corneal blink reflex suggests loss of the efferent pathway on this side. ls > Vv

after.stem: A 64 year old lady complains of a sore right eye. On examination, you note a normal corneal blink reflex on her left side but no consensual blink reflex on her right side. A lesion in which of the following structures is most likely to cause this clinical picture:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: The corneal reflex is afferent through the ophthalmic division of CN V and efferent through CN VII; loss of the right efferent limb causes absent right consensual blink.
after.learningNote: The corneal reflex is afferent through the ophthalmic division of CN V and efferent through CN VII; loss of the right efferent limb causes absent right consensual blink.
after.highYieldNote: The corneal reflex is afferent through the ophthalmic division of CN V and efferent through CN VII; loss of the right efferent limb causes absent right consensual blink.
after.mnemonic: V1 feels the cornea; VII closes the eye.

memoryAid.coreFact: The corneal reflex is afferent through the ophthalmic division of CN V and efferent through CN VII; loss of the right efferent limb causes absent right consensual blink.
memoryAid.mnemonic: V1 feels the cornea; VII closes the eye.

evidence.externalFinding: The facial-nerve reference supports CN VII as the efferent corneal-reflex pathway.

before.stem: Oculomotor (CN Ill) palsy with sparing of the pupillary reflex is most likely caused by which of the following:
options: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: Compressive causes of CN III palsy cause early pupillary dilatation because the parasympathetic fibres run peripherally in the nerve and are easily compressed. In diabetes mellitus the lesions are ischaemic rather than compressive and therefore typically affect the central fibres resulting in pupillary sparing. Vv

after.stem: Oculomotor (CN III) palsy with sparing of the pupillary reflex is most likely caused by which of the following:
options: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: Diabetic ischemic CN III palsy typically affects central motor fibres and may spare the peripheral parasympathetic pupillary fibres; compressive lesions more often dilate the pupil.
after.learningNote: Diabetic ischemic CN III palsy typically affects central motor fibres and may spare the peripheral parasympathetic pupillary fibres; compressive lesions more often dilate the pupil.
after.highYieldNote: Diabetic ischemic CN III palsy typically affects central motor fibres and may spare the peripheral parasympathetic pupillary fibres; compressive lesions more often dilate the pupil.
after.mnemonic: Diabetes keeps the pupil alive; compression opens it.

memoryAid.coreFact: Diabetic ischemic CN III palsy typically affects central motor fibres and may spare the peripheral parasympathetic pupillary fibres; compressive lesions more often dilate the pupil.
memoryAid.mnemonic: Diabetes keeps the pupil alive; compression opens it.

evidence.externalFinding: The oculomotor-nerve reference supports pupil-sparing diabetic ischemic palsy.

before.stem: Which of the following clinical features would you most expect to see in a glossopharyngeal nerve palsy:
options: Loss of jaw jerk 2% Loss of gag reflex 81%
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.
before.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve is the afferent pathway of the gag reflex. Tongue weakness and fasciculations may be seen in hypoglossal nerve palsy. Loss of jaw jerk may be seen in palsy of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Hoarseness and uvular deviation may been seen in vagus nerve palsy. Vv

after.stem: Which of the following clinical features would you most expect to see in a glossopharyngeal nerve palsy:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: CN IX is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, so glossopharyngeal palsy can cause loss of the gag reflex; uvular deviation and hoarseness are more associated with CN X.
after.learningNote: CN IX is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, so glossopharyngeal palsy can cause loss of the gag reflex; uvular deviation and hoarseness are more associated with CN X.
after.highYieldNote: CN IX is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, so glossopharyngeal palsy can cause loss of the gag reflex; uvular deviation and hoarseness are more associated with CN X.
after.mnemonic: IX initiates the gag; X executes the voice and palate.

memoryAid.coreFact: CN IX is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, so glossopharyngeal palsy can cause loss of the gag reflex; uvular deviation and hoarseness are more associated with CN X.
